items.stem: Foucault used Jeremy Bentham's design of the panopticon to illustrate:
options: how constant possible surveillance makes people discipline themselves
items.answer: how constant possible surveillance makes people discipline themselves
items.markingKey: D. Discipline and Punish (1975).

items.stem: Explain the difference between hegemony and coercion.
items.answer: Hegemony is domination through consent and common sense; coercion is domination through force or the threat of force. Gramsci argued that stable rule combines both.
items.markingKey: Hegemony is domination through consent and common sense; coercion is domination through force or the threat of force. Gramsci argued that stable rule combines both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why Scott argued that peasants rarely engage in open rebellion.
items.answer: Open rebellion is dangerous and usually crushed, so the poor use low-risk, anonymous everyday resistance that protects them while contesting exploitation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Open rebellion is dangerous and usually crushed, so the poor use low-risk, anonymous everyday resistance that protects them while contesting exploitation. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline how change shapes theories of power, hegemony and everyday resistance, using evidence from Scott's Weapons of the Weak.
items.answer: Green Revolution mechanisation transformed village relations, eroding customary obligations of the rich to employ the poor and give them alms (zakat).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Green Revolution mechanisation transformed village relations, eroding customary obligations of the rich to employ the poor and give them alms (zakat). Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (James C. Scott, Weapons of the Weak: Everyday Forms of Peasant Resistance (1985), in "Sedaka", a pseudonymous rice-growing village in Kedah, Malaysia (fieldwork 1978–1980)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to change. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Mei writes: "If people do not openly protest, they must accept their domination." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Scott showed that apparent compliance can mask hidden transcripts and everyday resistance.
items.markingKey: Scott showed that apparent compliance can mask hidden transcripts and everyday resistance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the garment factory, each sewing line has a screen that shows its output against the hourly target in red or green. Supervisors walk behind the women but rarely speak; the screen speaks for them. During the afternoon shift, Shapla's line falls into red. The women do not complain. Instead, at exactly 4 p.m., all twelve go to the toilet together, "because we are sisters". The line stays red for ten minutes. The supervisor writes nothing down. The next morning, the target on the screen has been lowered slightly.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a garment factory in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

Analyse how the text illustrates both disciplinary power and everyday resistance. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: The screen is a Foucauldian device: constant visible measurement makes workers discipline themselves without supervisors speaking. The collective toilet break is everyday resistance (Scott): an indirect, deniable act ("because we are sisters") that disrupts production without open protest, and it works – the target is lowered – showing power negotiated within the factory.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The screen is a Foucauldian device: constant visible measurement makes workers discipline themselves without supervisors speaking. The collective toilet break is everyday resistance (Scott): an indirect, deniable act ("because we are sisters") that disrupts production without open protest, and it works – the target is lowered – showing power negotiated within the factory. items.stem: Compare and contrast Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice and Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline as accounts of theories of power, hegemony and everyday resistance, focusing on the key concept of space, place and time.
items.answer: Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice (based on fieldwork among the Kabyle of Algeria (1950s–1960s)): The Kabyle house is organised by oppositions (male/female, light/dark, high/low), so moving through domestic space inscribes the gender order in the body. Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline (among young Malay women working in Japanese-owned electronics factories in Kuala Langat, Selangor, Malaysia (late 1970s)): Factories imposed clock time and spatial control – bounded workstations, microscopes, supervisors – that clashed with the rhythms of village life. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far space, place and time is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Explain why Gramsci's concept of hegemony helps explain why the powerless often do not rebel.
items.answer: If the dominant group's values come to seem natural and common sense through education, religion and media, subordinates consent to their position, so domination rests on persuasion as well as force.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If the dominant group's values come to seem natural and common sense through education, religion and media, subordinates consent to their position, so domination rests on persuasion as well as force. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between everyday resistance and open rebellion.
items.answer: Everyday resistance is hidden, individual or informal action that avoids direct confrontation; open rebellion is collective, public challenge to authority, such as uprisings or strikes.
items.markingKey: Everyday resistance is hidden, individual or informal action that avoids direct confrontation; open rebellion is collective, public challenge to authority, such as uprisings or strikes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Scott's "Sedaka" shows everyday resistance.
items.answer: After combine harvesters replaced hand harvesting, poor villagers gossiped about stingy rich farmers, pilfered rice and dragged their feet, while publicly showing deference. The poor contested the new economic order and its moral justification without risking open confrontation.
items.markingKey: Context (After combine harvesters replaced hand harvesting, poor villagers gossiped about stingy rich farmers, pilfered rice and dragged their feet, while publicly showing deference.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the poor contested the new economic order and its moral justification without risking open confrontation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to everyday resistance.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Processes by which divided communities and individuals rebuild relationships after violence"?
items.answer: reconciliation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of reconciliation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the concept of a continuum of violence is useful.
items.answer: It links everyday and structural violence (poverty, racism) to direct political violence, showing how normalised suffering can prepare the ground for atrocity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It links everyday and structural violence (poverty, racism) to direct political violence, showing how normalised suffering can prepare the ground for atrocity. items.stem: Explain the difference between direct violence and everyday violence.
items.answer: Direct violence is physical harm inflicted in war, repression or crime; everyday violence (Scheper-Hughes) is the routine, normalised suffering of poverty and humiliation that people come to see as ordinary.
items.markingKey: Direct violence is physical harm inflicted in war, repression or crime; everyday violence (Scheper-Hughes) is the routine, normalised suffering of poverty and humiliation that people come to see as ordinary. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Every year on 7 April the school in the hills holds a commemoration. The children, born long after 1994, recite names of the dead in Kinyarwanda. Mukamana, a survivor, sits at the front; three rows behind her sits Jean-Paul, who served his sentence for taking part in the killings and now farms the next field. They greet each other at the market. "We share a well," Mukamana tells me. "I do not forget. But I need water." After the ceremony, the headteacher asks the children not to talk about "ethnic" groups: "Here, we are all Rwandan."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Rwanda.

Identify and describe what happens at the commemoration and afterwards. Refer closely to the text. Refer to at least three specific details from the text.
items.answer: Children born after 1994 recite names of the dead in Kinyarwanda; Mukamana, a survivor, sits at the front and Jean-Paul, a released perpetrator who now farms the next field, sits three rows behind; they greet each other at the market and share a well; the headteacher tells the children not to talk about ethnic groups.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Once a war ends, violence ends too." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Structural, domestic and criminal violence often continue, and the effects of war persist in bodies, memories and relationships.
items.markingKey: Structural, domestic and criminal violence often continue, and the effects of war persist in bodies, memories and relationships. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that truth commissions are more effective than local practices in achieving reconciliation. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Both are needed: national acknowledgement and local relational repair.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: they produce national acknowledgement and records (Peru TRC); they can recommend reparations; local rituals and confessions repair relationships between neighbours (Theidon); commissions may not reach rural people or address daily coexistence. Suitable ethnographies include Theidon's Intimate Enemies, Das's Life and Words, Nordstrom's A Different Kind of War Story. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Both are needed: national acknowledgement and local relational repair. items.stem: Outline how social relations shapes violence, conflict and the state, using evidence from Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping.
items.answer: Facing very high infant mortality, some mothers delayed emotional attachment to babies judged weak and let them die "without weeping" – a contested argument about how scarcity shapes maternal love.

Compare the significance of power in the text with its significance in Malkki's Purity and Exile. Refer explicitly to the ethnographic context of both. Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: Victim and perpetrator are "intimate enemies" (Theidon) living as neighbours; Mukamana's pragmatic coexistence ("I need water") shows reconciliation through everyday necessity rather than forgiveness (Das's descent into the ordinary); state-led memory (annual commemoration) and the ban on ethnic labels show power shaping how violence is remembered and how identities are classified. items.answer: self-determination

items.stem: Hana writes: "Social movements succeed only if they win their demands immediately." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Movements can change public discourse, build identities and alliances, and influence law over the long term even without immediate victories.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why global connections can strengthen local resistance.
items.answer: Alliances with NGOs, environmentalists, media and international law give local movements resources and visibility (Tsing's Meratus alliances; Zapatista use of the internet), though they also bring unequal power. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The meeting in the longhouse lasts until midnight. The mining company has offered a new school and jobs in exchange for consent to survey the hills. Young people argue that the jobs are needed; the elders say the hills hold their ancestors' graves. A lawyer from an NGO in the capital explains "free, prior and informed consent" in the national language, and a schoolteacher translates. At the end, the community decides to delay. "They want us to say yes or no," says Grandmother Bua. "We say: not yet. We will ask the hills."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an Indigenous community in Sarawak, Malaysia.

Using the key concept of power, explain how the text illustrates the politics of Indigenous rights and consent. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: International norms of FPIC are mediated by outsiders (NGO lawyer, translation), giving the community leverage; internal disagreement (youth wanting jobs vs elders defending graves) shows the community is not homogeneous; "not yet" refuses the company's binary framing, asserting the community's own time and relationship to land.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: International norms of FPIC are mediated by outsiders (NGO lawyer, translation), giving the community leverage; internal disagreement (youth wanting jobs vs elders defending graves) shows the community is not homogeneous; "not yet" refuses the company's binary framing, asserting the community's own time and relationship to land. items.stem:
Read the text below.

The documentary crew arrived in the village for three days. They asked the women to grind maize "the old way" on a stone, although most use the mill now. Rosa refused: "We are not a museum." Her cousin agreed, for a fee, and wore her grandmother's embroidered blouse. When the film was shown in the capital, the narrator described the village as "untouched by time". Rosa's son, a university student, posted a video reply showing the mill, his phone and his mother's market stall, which was shared thousands of times.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a Maya village in highland Guatemala.

With reference to the concept of power, analyse how the text raises questions about power and representation. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.

items.stem: Explain why representations in ethnography can have real effects on the people described.
items.answer: Images such as the "fierce" Yanomami or "culture of poverty" can influence policy, media and how others treat the group, affecting land rights, aid and discrimination.

items.stem: "Only members of a community should write ethnographies about it." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Insider ethnography is valuable and overdue, but representation is best improved through collaboration and reflexivity rather than exclusion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: insiders have deeper access and accountability (Hurston, Simpson); outsiders have historically misrepresented. Arguments against: outsiders can notice what insiders take for granted; communities are diverse, so insiders also speak for others; collaboration combines strengths. Supported judgement: Insider ethnography is valuable and overdue, but representation is best improved through collaboration and reflexivity rather than exclusion. items.answer: Retributive justice punishes perpetrators through courts; restorative justice seeks to repair relationships through acknowledgement, confession and reconciliation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Every year on 7 April the school in the hills holds a commemoration. The children, born long after 1994, recite names of the dead in Kinyarwanda. Mukamana, a survivor, sits at the front; three rows behind her sits Jean-Paul, who served his sentence for taking part in the killings and now farms the next field. They greet each other at the market. "We share a well," Mukamana tells me. "I do not forget. But I need water." After the ceremony, the headteacher asks the children not to talk about "ethnic" groups: "Here, we are all Rwandan."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Rwanda.

Using the key concept of power, explain how the text illustrates coexistence after political violence. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: Victim and perpetrator are "intimate enemies" (Theidon) living as neighbours; Mukamana's pragmatic coexistence ("I need water") shows reconciliation through everyday necessity rather than forgiveness (Das's descent into the ordinary); state-led memory (annual commemoration) and the ban on ethnic labels show power shaping how violence is remembered and how identities are classified.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Yanomami controversy and explain what it reveals about representation and its consequences.
items.answer: Chagnon's portrayal of the Yanomami as "the fierce people" was criticised for supporting claims that they were violent and did not deserve protected land. The image created by an ethnography travelled beyond academia and was used in political debates about Yanomami territory.

At the garment factory, each sewing line has a screen that shows its output against the hourly target in red or green. Supervisors walk behind the women but rarely speak; the screen speaks for them. During the afternoon shift, Shapla's line falls into red. The women do not complain. Instead, at exactly 4 p.m., all twelve go to the toilet together, "because we are sisters". The line stays red for ten minutes. The supervisor writes nothing down. The next morning, the target on the screen has been lowered slightly.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a garment factory in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

items.stem: Briefly describe Das's Life and Words and explain what it reveals about violence and the everyday.
items.answer: Women who had been abducted or violated during Partition rebuilt their lives quietly within families, often without speaking publicly. Healing occurred through a "descent into the ordinary" – small acts of care – rather than public testimony.

The meeting in the longhouse lasts until midnight. The mining company has offered a new school and jobs in exchange for consent to survey the hills. Young people argue that the jobs are needed; the elders say the hills hold their ancestors' graves. A lawyer from an NGO in the capital explains "free, prior and informed consent" in the national language, and a schoolteacher translates. At the end, the community decides to delay. "They want us to say yes or no," says Grandmother Bua. "We say: not yet. We will ask the hills."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an Indigenous community in Sarawak, Malaysia.

The documentary crew arrived in the village for three days. They asked the women to grind maize "the old way" on a stone, although most use the mill now. Rosa refused: "We are not a museum." Her cousin agreed, for a fee, and wore her grandmother's embroidered blouse. When the film was shown in the capital, the narrator described the village as "untouched by time". Rosa's son, a university student, posted a video reply showing the mill, his phone and his mother's market stall, which was shared thousands of times.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a Maya village in highland Guatemala.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Foucault's view of power is more useful to anthropologists than Gramsci's."
items.answer: Each illuminates different dimensions; ethnographers often combine Foucault's discipline with Gramsci's hegemony.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Foucault shows power everywhere in institutions and bodies; it explains discipline in schools, prisons, factories. Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. You may refer to ethical codes, but apply them to the situation described.

items.stem: Compare and contrast Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus and Nash's Mayan Visions as accounts of social movements, Indigenous rights and resistance, focusing on the key concept of identity.
items.answer: Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus (in Kahnawà:ke, a Mohawk community near Montreal, Canada): Simpson is herself from Kahnawà:ke and practises "ethnographic refusal", declining to publish some internal matters. items.answer: Everyday resistance is hidden, individual or informal action that avoids direct confrontation; open rebellion is collective, public challenge to authority, such as uprisings or strikes.

items.stem: Using the Standing Rock protests (2016–2017) as an example, explain Indigenous rights and resistance.
items.answer: The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe and thousands of supporters camped near the Missouri River to oppose the Dakota Access Pipeline, under the slogan "Mni Wiconi" ("water is life"). The protest combined defence of water and sacred sites with assertions of treaty rights and drew global solidarity, though the pipeline was completed.

items.answer: Chagnon's portrayal of the Yanomami as "the fierce people" was criticised for supporting claims that they were violent and did not deserve protected land. The image created by an ethnography travelled beyond academia and was used in political debates about Yanomami territory.

Read the text below.

At the garment factory, each sewing line has a screen that shows its output against the hourly target in red or green. Supervisors walk behind the women but rarely speak; the screen speaks for them. During the afternoon shift, Shapla's line falls into red. The women do not complain. Instead, at exactly 4 p.m., all twelve go to the toilet together, "because we are sisters". The line stays red for ten minutes. The supervisor writes nothing down. The next morning, the target on the screen has been lowered slightly.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a garment factory in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.
items.answer: Workers could be dismissed if their coordinated action is identified; the factory, line and individuals must be anonymised; the anthropologist's presence on the shop floor may require management permission, which raises issues of trust with workers. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: "Social relations is central to understanding violence, conflict and the state." Compare and contrast two anthropological studies, for example Nordstrom's A Different Kind of War Story and Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, in the light of this claim.
items.answer: Nordstrom's A Different Kind of War Story (in Mozambique during the civil war (fieldwork 1988–1996)): Ordinary people, healers and communities resisted violence by rebuilding relationships and treating the wounds of war, including through rituals that cleansed returning fighters. Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping (among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)): Facing very high infant mortality, some mothers delayed emotional attachment to babies judged weak and let them die "without weeping" – a contested argument about how scarcity shapes maternal love. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far social relations is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that Indigenous rights movements have been largely successful. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: They have won important recognition but material control over land remains contested and uneven.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: UNDRIP (2007) and national recognition of land rights; greater visibility and political voice; extractive projects continue (Standing Rock pipeline completed); recognition can be limited or conditional; many communities remain impoverished. Suitable ethnographies include Simpson's Mohawk Interruptus, Tsing's Friction, Nash's Mayan Visions. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: They have won important recognition but material control over land remains contested and uneven. Read the text below.

The documentary crew arrived in the village for three days. They asked the women to grind maize "the old way" on a stone, although most use the mill now. Rosa refused: "We are not a museum." Her cousin agreed, for a fee, and wore her grandmother's embroidered blouse. When the film was shown in the capital, the narrator described the village as "untouched by time". Rosa's son, a university student, posted a video reply showing the mill, his phone and his mother's market stall, which was shared thousands of times.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a Maya village in highland Guatemala.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.
items.answer: Payment for staged performance raises issues of authenticity and consent; the anthropologist should avoid adding another layer of misrepresentation, seek permission from Rosa, her cousin and son, and consider the effect of publishing their names alongside the viral video. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
